title: The Dip
author: Seth Godin
short_description: Seth Godin on strategic quitting — recognize the Dip, quit the wrong things, and push through where mastery pays.
content_text:
PART 1 — KEY LESSONS (OUTLINE)

1. Markets reward being the best in a defined world

  • “Best in the world” means best for a specific audience with a real choice — not literally best on the planet. Scarcity of excellence concentrates attention, trust, and premium outcomes on those who finish where others stop.

2. The Dip is the hard valley between beginner gains and mastery

  • Early progress feels easy, then difficulty rises, feedback slows, and most people quit. That valley is the Dip: temporary pain that screens out competitors and makes the other side valuable.

3. Cul-de-sacs and cliffs are not Dips — quit them

  • A cul-de-sac is busy work with no path to better outcomes. A cliff looks fine until a sudden drop. Neither rewards persistence; recognizing them early is a skill.

4. Quitting can be a strategy, not a character flaw

  • Failing is quitting without a plan after resources are spent. Strategic quitting frees time, pride, and attention for Dips worth finishing. Never quit is often a slogan that keeps people stuck.

5. Map Dips in school, jobs, and craft before you commit

  • Every field has predictable hard stretches — certifications, sales cycles, creative droughts. Seeing the map in advance lets you choose whether the payoff justifies the climb.

6. Scarcity created by the Dip is why winners win

  • If everyone finished easily, excellence would be common and cheap. The Dip’s difficulty is what creates short supply of the best — and therefore demand for those who cross it.

7. Serial quitting beats fake grit when the path is dead

  • Grit is powerful inside the right Dip and destructive inside a cul-de-sac. Successful people often quit many low-leverage things early so they can stay longer where staying matters.

8. Pride and sunk cost keep people in the wrong curve

  • Ego hates the story “I quit.” Markets do not care about your story; they care about trajectory. Leaving a dead end is not betrayal of past effort — it is respect for future effort.

PART 2 — THE DIP

A 26-Minute Read Summary

Chapter 1: Being the best in the world (market)

Seth Godin opens with a claim that sounds arrogant until he defines it carefully: in almost every market that matters, people prefer the best option available to them. Not the tenth-best. Not the vaguely good enough option that tried hard. The best. That preference concentrates rewards — attention, referrals, pricing power, career opportunities — on a small set of winners. Mediocrity is crowded. Excellence is scarce. The book’s project is to explain why that scarcity exists and how strategic quitting helps you reach it.

“Best in the world” is intentionally provocative, then immediately narrowed. Godin does not mean you must beat every human on earth at every skill. He means best in the world that your customer, client, hiring manager, or audience actually considers. A local orthodontist can be the best in a zip code. A podcast can be the best for a narrow niche. A salesperson can be the best for one product line inside one industry. The relevant “world” is the set of alternatives a decision-maker compares. Shrink the world honestly, and “best” becomes a strategy rather than a fantasy.

This framing attacks a comforting myth: that effort alone is enough, and that being “pretty good” at many things is a safe life plan. Pretty good is where most competition lives. Pretty good is easy to replace. Pretty good rarely gets the shortlist, the premium fee, or the lasting reputation. Godin’s point is economic as much as motivational. When buyers have limited time and limited trust, they simplify. They choose the option that feels like the winner in their category. If you are not aiming to become that option in some defined market, you are volunteering to compete in the overcrowded middle.

Being best is also temporary and contextual. Markets move. Categories redefine. A winner who stops improving can lose the title. So the aspiration is not a trophy you polish once; it is a standard you defend with ongoing work. The rest of the book asks a harder question: which struggles are worth finishing because they lead to that scarce position, and which struggles should be abandoned because they never will?

Lesson: Aim to be the best in a clearly defined market, because buyers concentrate rewards on winners and leave the crowded middle underpaid and replaceable.

Chapter 2: The Dip defined

The Dip is Godin’s name for the long, difficult valley between starting something and mastering it. At the beginning, progress is often fast. You learn the basics, get early wins, feel smart. Then the curve bends. Improvement slows. The work gets harder. Feedback becomes less frequent or less flattering. Competitors who were casually interested start dropping out. That stretch — where effort rises and visible payoff lags — is the Dip.

The Dip is not random suffering. It is a filter. Systems that matter tend to have a Dip because if excellence were easy, everyone would have it and it would stop being valuable. Medical residencies, sales quotas, athletic training, building a trusted brand, writing a body of work people rely on — each has a period where the cost of continuing feels disproportionate to short-term reward. People who quit in that valley leave opportunity for those who stay.

Godin wants you to see the Dip as information, not as a personal verdict. Feeling stuck does not automatically mean you chose wrong. Feeling stuck may mean you have reached the part of the curve that separates dabblers from professionals. The emotional texture of the Dip includes boredom, doubt, comparison, and the temptation to start something newer and easier. Those feelings are predictable. Treating them as surprising moral failures makes you more likely to quit the wrong things for the wrong reasons.

Importantly, the Dip assumes an eventual upturn: if you keep going with skill and resources, outcomes improve and scarcity begins to pay. That assumption is what distinguishes a Dip from a dead end. In a true Dip, extra effort still has a path to better results. The pain is real, but it is not pointless. The book’s later chapters help you test whether the path exists before you romanticize endurance.

A practical way to recognize a Dip: Are people quitting here for reasons that do not erase the prize? Did early progress exist, then flatten, while a second wave of skill is still possible? Would finishing create credentials, trust, or capability beginners cannot fake? If yes, the valley is doing economic work, not merely tormenting you.

Godin also implies that Dips have different lengths and depths. Some last weeks; some last years. Misjudging depth is how people either quit too soon or stay too long without a plan. Naming the Dip does not remove the pain. It gives you a category so you can decide consciously: lean in, redesign your approach, or leave because this is not a Dip after all.

Lesson: Treat the hard valley after easy beginnings as a Dip — a temporary filter that creates scarcity — and judge it by whether continued skilled effort can still produce a real upturn.

Chapter 3: The cul-de-sac and the cliff

Not every hard situation is a Dip. Godin introduces two other curves that demand a different response: the cul-de-sac and the cliff. A cul-de-sac is a dead end that keeps you busy without improving your prospects. You work, you show up, you even get occasional praise, but the trajectory does not bend toward “best in the world” in any market that matters. Effort goes in; asymmetric upside does not come out. Persistence in a cul-de-sac is not grit. It is a slow leak of your career.

Cul-de-sacs are dangerous because they feel responsible. A stable job with no growth path, a side project that never finds an audience no matter how you iterate, a relationship with a market that cannot pay, a role where politics permanently block advancement — these can look like loyalty from the inside. From the outside, they look like avoidance of a harder choice. Godin’s blunt advice is to quit cul-de-sacs as soon as you recognize them. Staying to “see it through” only makes sense if there is a through.

The cliff is different. Things seem fine, even successful, until a sudden drop: a market collapse, a regulatory change, a business model that was secretly fragile, a habit that works until it destroys health or reputation. Cliffs are harder to see in advance, which is why Godin emphasizes pattern recognition and skepticism about strategies that only work until they catastrophically fail. If the curve you are on depends on denial — “this will never catch up with me” — you may be walking toward a cliff rather than climbing through a Dip.

The diagnostic skill is simple to say and hard to practice: ask whether additional effort can improve outcomes in a meaningful way. In a Dip, yes. In a cul-de-sac, no — more effort mostly produces more of the same. On a cliff, effort may even accelerate the fall if it deepens commitment to a brittle path. Labeling your situation correctly is the first strategic move. Many people apply Dip advice to cul-de-sacs and then conclude that all persistence advice is a lie. They had the wrong curve.

Lesson: Quit cul-de-sacs and respect cliffs; reserve persistence for true Dips where more skilled effort can still change the outcome.

Chapter 4: Quitting as strategy

Godin’s most countercultural move is to rehabilitate quitting. Culture often treats quitting as moral failure and persistence as virtue in every context. The Dip argues that this is backwards when the path is wrong. Strategic quitting is a decision made early enough, clearly enough, and for reasons tied to opportunity cost. Failing, in Godin’s contrast, is what happens when you drip away resources, pride, and time until you are forced out without a plan. Quitting is a choice. Failing is a verdict delivered by exhaustion.

Strategic quitters ask better questions before and during a project: What does winning look like? Is this a Dip, a cul-de-sac, or a cliff? If I quit, what will I do with the freed capacity? If I stay, what specific skills and milestones prove I am moving through the valley rather than jogging in place? Persistence without those questions is not strategy. It is inertia wearing a motivational poster.

Quitting also needs timing. Quitting at the first discomfort means you never enter any Dip worth taking. Quitting after you have already paid most of the cost without changing the destination wastes the sunk cost twice — once in the past, and again by refusing to reallocate what remains. The art is to quit when new information shows the curve is wrong, or when a better Dip appears that you cannot pursue while trapped in a dead end. That is not flakiness. That is portfolio management for a finite life.

Godin is not celebrating quitters who abandon people, ethics, or commitments casually. He is attacking the superstition that finishing every started thing is inherently noble. Markets do not award medals for completed cul-de-sacs. They award outcomes. A person who quits three mediocre jobs to build rare skill in one craft may look inconsistent on a resume line and still be strategically coherent. A person who never quits anything may look loyal and still be stuck.

Timing still matters. Quit at the first discomfort and you never enter a Dip worth taking. Quit only after every resource is gone and you have merely failed without a plan. The art is to leave when new information shows the curve is wrong, or when a better Dip appears that you cannot pursue while trapped in a dead end.

Lesson: Treat quitting as a strategic reallocation of effort — decide early with clear criteria — rather than failing by drifting until you are forced out.

Chapter 5: Education, jobs, and Dip maps

Godin invites readers to map Dips in familiar domains so the pattern becomes recognizable before emotions take over. Education has classic Dips: the middle of a difficult degree, the grind of licensing exams, the years when expertise is forming but credentials and income have not yet caught up. Students who quit in those valleys often do so when the Dip is doing exactly what it is designed to do — separating casual enrollment from earned capability. That does not mean every program is worth finishing. It means you should know whether you are in a Dip toward a scarce skill or a cul-de-sac degree that the market no longer values.

Jobs and careers have Dip maps too. The first months in a sales role can feel hopeful; then rejection stacks up; then a smaller group learns the craft and begins to close. Creative careers often show early novelty, then a long stretch of invisible practice, then a reputation inflection. Entrepreneurship has fundraising Dips, distribution Dips, and hiring Dips. If you enter a field without a rough map of where people usually quit, you will interpret normal valley pain as a unique sign you are doomed.

Dip maps are also honesty tools. Talk to people who finished. Ask where they almost left. Ask what skills actually moved the needle. Ask which parts of the folklore were theater. A good map does not remove the Dip; it prevents you from being surprised by it. Surprise is what turns temporary difficulty into panic quitting. Anticipation turns the same difficulty into a scheduled phase.

Build your map in three columns: entry rewards, valley demands, and post-Dip scarcity. Entry rewards are what seduce beginners — status, excitement, easy early wins. Valley demands are the skills, hours, capital, or emotional stamina required mid-curve. Post-Dip scarcity is what the market actually pays for — board certification, a portfolio clients trust, distribution muscle, a sales book of business. If you cannot fill the third column, beware. A path with a painful middle and no scarce prize is often a cul-de-sac with better storytelling.

Lesson: Chart where Dips usually appear in your education and career so you can choose valleys that lead to scarce value instead of being shocked into quitting — or into staying in a dead end.

Chapter 6: Scarcity and the Dip’s value

Why does the Dip matter economically? Because it creates scarcity, and scarcity creates value. If becoming excellent were comfortable and short, excellence would be common. When excellence is common, buyers pay less and care less. The Dip is painful precisely so that fewer people finish. Those who finish enter a thinner competitive field. That thinness is the prize.

Godin’s scarcity argument reframes discomfort. The ache of the Dip is not merely an obstacle between you and success; it is part of the reason success pays. A certification that everyone gets overnight stops signaling. A brand that everyone can clone overnight stops commanding loyalty. A skill that requires years of deliberate practice remains rare, and rare skills can be priced, trusted, and sought. The Dip is a moat that forms while you climb.

This is why quitting at the bottom can be so costly. The bottom is where scarcity is being manufactured. Many people leave just before the curve turns, which means they paid Dip tuition without collecting Dip rent. Godin is not promising that every valley ends in riches. He is explaining why the valleys that do lead to “best in the world” outcomes are valuable: because most people will not cross them.

Scarcity also explains market behavior around winners. Once someone is perceived as best in a category, attention compounds. Referrals preferentially go to the known excellent option. Media simplifies stories around leaders. That post-Dip compounding is unavailable to those who settle for permanent almost. The strategic implication is sharp: either commit to crossing a Dip that produces real scarcity, or quit early and move to a different Dip. Occupying the almost-zone forever is how people work hard without becoming scarce.

Do not confuse artificial pain with valuable scarcity. Bureaucracy that blocks you without building skill is friction without payoff. A valuable Dip produces capability, trust, or distribution others lack. If the valley only produces trauma and jargon, reconsider. Markets pay for scarce usefulness, not for proof that you suffered.

Lesson: Embrace that the Dip’s difficulty creates scarce excellence — the very scarcity that makes being best in a market valuable — and avoid paying the cost without aiming for that prize.

Chapter 7: Serial quitting vs grit myths

Popular culture often sells a single story: winners never quit. Godin’s counter-story is that winners quit a lot — just not in the Dip that matters. Serial strategic quitting clears the calendar for extraordinary persistence where persistence has leverage. The opposite pattern is also common: people who never quit anything, spreading themselves across cul-de-sacs, hobbies without markets, and obligations that defend ego rather than build scarce skill.

Grit myths become harmful when they are context-blind. Grit inside a true Dip toward a chosen market is a competitive advantage. Grit inside a cul-de-sac is self-harm with good PR. The same personality trait can produce mastery or stagnation depending on the curve underneath it. Godin wants discernment paired with courage: courage to stay, and courage to leave.

Serial quitters look restless to observers who worship consistency theater. But consistency theater — showing up forever to the wrong thing — is not the same as consistency of purpose. Purpose may require abandoning paths that no longer serve the aim of becoming best somewhere that matters. The resume may have discontinuities. The strategy may still be linear: keep reallocating toward scarce, valuable mastery.

This chapter also challenges the addiction to starting. Starting is fun; Dips are not. Some people quit at the first Dip and restart elsewhere, collecting beginnings like trophies. That is not strategic quitting; that is Dip avoidance. The test is whether you quit because the path is a cul-de-sac or cliff, or because the Dip began doing its job. If you always leave when boredom and difficulty arrive, you will never become scarce. If you never leave when growth is impossible, you will also never become scarce. Both errors are expensive.

Watch your pattern. Quitting every valley after boredom arrives is Dip avoidance, not strategy. Never quitting across years of flat results is grit mythology. Accurate quitting clears space; accurate persistence creates scarcity. The goal is not a high or low quit count — it is the right quit at the right curve.

Lesson: Practice serial strategic quitting of dead ends so you can apply real grit only to Dips where staying creates scarce, marketable excellence.

Chapter 8: When pride keeps you stuck

Pride is one of the main reasons people refuse to quit cul-de-sacs. Quitting threatens the story they have told colleagues, family, and themselves: I am the kind of person who finishes. I have already invested so much. I would look foolish if I stopped now. Godin treats those stories with skepticism. Markets are not obligated to repay pride. Sunk costs are real historically and irrelevant economically. The money, years, and identity invested in a dead end cannot be recovered by investing more.

Pride also confuses temporary Dip pain with humiliation. In a Dip, you may feel average, rejected, or invisible for a stretch. That feeling can be part of the filter. Pride wants applause on a schedule. Mastery often withholds applause until scarcity appears. If you use pride as your only compass, you will exit valuable Dips to protect short-term image, and you will stay in cul-de-sacs to protect long-term image. Both moves optimize for narrative comfort over outcome.

A practical antidote is to replace “What will people think if I quit?” with “What will my future market position be if I stay?” Another antidote is to pre-define success metrics that are about trajectory, not face-saving: skills acquired, customers earned, measurable quality, proximity to best-in-world status in your niche. If metrics are flat and unfixable, pride is a poor reason to continue. If metrics are hard but bending upward, prideful impatience is a poor reason to leave.

Godin’s tone here is compassionate but firm. He understands why people stay. He refuses to call that loyalty “strategy.” The kindest move for your future self is sometimes a quit that embarrasses your past self. Embarrassment is a short cost. Misallocated decades are a long one.

Pride wears costumes: “I owe it to the team,” “I’m so close,” “I’ve always been a fighter.” Ask an outsider who is not invested in your story whether they would stay. Healthy pride protects craft and promises that still make sense. Unhealthy pride refuses to revise a decision even when the curve is dead.

Lesson: Do not let ego and sunk-cost pride trap you in cul-de-sacs — judge paths by future trajectory, not by how foolish quitting might look today.

Chapter 9: Choosing your Dip carefully

Because Dips are expensive, Godin insists you choose them on purpose. Not every difficult path leads to a market that will care. Not every market that cares is one where you can realistically become best. The strategic life is a matching problem: your resources and tastes on one side, a Dip that produces scarce value on the other. Entering random hard things because hardship feels virtuous is a misunderstanding of the book.

Choosing carefully means asking several questions before you lean in. Is there a real customer or audience at the end? Does finishing create scarcity, or just a certificate everyone has? Can I access the training, capital, time, and support this Dip requires? Do I want the life that comes with being best in this micro-world — the travel, the stress, the type of workdays it produces? A Dip you secretly hate even after success is a poor allocation, even if it is prestigious.

Godin also implies focus. Crossing one meaningful Dip often requires quitting lesser ones. Parallel Dips can dilute the persistence each valley requires. The people who look “lucky” on the far side usually concentrated. They said no to side quests that would have been fine stories and bad strategies. Choosing a Dip is therefore also choosing what you will not pursue for a season.

This chapter connects back to “best in the world.” Pick a world small enough that bestness is achievable and valuable enough that bestness matters. A tiny world with no demand is a hobby. A huge world where you cannot differentiate is a fantasy. The fertile middle is a defined market with room for an exceptional offer. Your Dip should be the training ground for that offer.

Before you lean in, run a short pre-check: What wrong reasons might make you quit at the bottom, and what supports will counter them? What right reasons should make you exit — market disappearance, misfit, ethics — and how will you keep those exit ramps visible so pride cannot hide them later?

Lesson: Select Dips deliberately where you can become best in a valuable defined market, and drop competing pursuits that would dilute the persistence that valley requires.

Chapter 10: Quitting the wrong audience

Sometimes the product, craft, or career path is fine, but the audience is wrong. Godin, a marketer by trade, emphasizes that sticking with people who do not want what you offer is a special kind of cul-de-sac. You can improve endlessly and still get no traction if you are performing for a market that is indifferent, unable to pay, or culturally mismatched. In those cases, quitting the audience — not quitting the skill — is the strategic move.

Wrong-audience persistence looks like hustle. You post more, discount more, plead more, and call the lack of response a Dip. But a Dip assumes that continued excellence eventually meets demand. If demand is structurally absent, you are pushing a boulder sideways. The fix may be repositioning: a different niche, a different geographic market, a different customer segment, a different promise. That can feel like quitting because you abandon a familiar crowd. It is often the moment the real Dip begins — the Dip of serving people who actually care.

This distinction protects creators and professionals from false lessons. “I guess I’m not good enough” may be true, or it may mean “I showed my work to people who were never going to buy.” Testing audiences is part of strategic quitting. Short experiments, clear offers, honest metrics. If one segment leans in, lean into their Dip. If none do, reconsider the offer itself. What you should not do is marry the first audience that noticed you if they cannot sustain a market for excellence.

Quitting the wrong audience also applies inside organizations. Maybe your company will never value the craft you want to master. Staying forever to convince the unconvincible can be pride. Leaving for a team that needs that craft can be strategy. The skill continues; the context changes. Godin’s framework supports that kind of quit because the aim is not to endure every room. The aim is to become best in a world that recognizes the win.

Lesson: Quit audiences and contexts that cannot value your work, and move your craft to a market where becoming best is both possible and rewarded.

Chapter 11: Pushing through the right Dip

Once you have chosen a real Dip — right market, right curve, right scarcity — Godin’s advice flips from quitting to intensifying. The middle of the Dip is where extra effort has unusual leverage because so many others are leaving. This is not a call to reckless overwork. It is a call to raise the quality and seriousness of your practice when average effort will not create best-in-world outcomes.

Pushing through means better coaches, tighter feedback loops, more deliberate practice, and fewer distractions — not merely longer hours of the same ineffective motions. If you are in a sales Dip, it may mean improving discovery questions and pipeline discipline. If you are in a writing Dip, it may mean shipping on a schedule and studying structure, not waiting for inspiration. If you are in a fitness or skill Dip, it may mean progressive training with measurement. The Dip rewards improved approach under pressure, not performative suffering.

Mindset matters here, but as fuel for process, not as magic. Expect the valley. Normalize the boredom. Keep the market definition visible so you remember why the pain is worth it. Celebrate leading indicators — skill checks, customer conversations, quality scores — when lagging indicators like fame or revenue are still quiet. People who survive Dips usually become obsessed with controllables.

Community helps when it is the right community: peers who are also crossing, mentors who have finished, standards that make quitting-for-convenience socially expensive and quitting-for-strategy socially acceptable. The wrong community glamorizes burnout or mocks ambition. Choose witnesses carefully.

Godin’s insistence on being best also shapes how you push. You are not trying to survive the Dip as a permanent resident. You are trying to exit into scarcity. That means periodically asking whether your practice still points at differentiation. Busy valleys can become cul-de-sacs if you stop aiming at excellence and start aiming only at endurance. Push through, but push through toward a sharper offer, a rarer skill, a clearer claim to best in your world.

Lesson: When you are in the right Dip, intensify deliberate practice and raise standards as others leave, aiming at scarce excellence rather than mere endurance.

Chapter 12: Your Dip decision worksheet

The Dip becomes useful when it turns into a decision tool you can reuse. End with a practical worksheet mindset Godin’s ideas support, even in paraphrased form. For any commitment that is consuming serious time, walk through a short sequence in writing — not in your head, where pride edits the answers.

First, name the market. Who is the customer or audience? What world are they comparing you within? What would “best” mean in their language — fastest results, most trusted taste, most reliable delivery, deepest expertise? If you cannot name the market, you are not in a strategy yet. Second, name the curve. Is this a Dip with a plausible upturn, a cul-de-sac with busy motion, or a cliff with hidden fragility? Write the evidence, not the hope. Third, name the scarcity. If you finish, what will be rare about you? If nothing, why are you paying Dip prices?

Fourth, run the pride check. What sunk cost or image threat is biasing you toward staying or leaving? Discount that bias on purpose. Fifth, run the opportunity-cost check. What alternative Dip could you enter with the same resources? Is it better? Sixth, decide: quit, switch audience, or lean in. If you lean in, write the next three practice upgrades and the metrics that will prove movement over the next sixty to ninety days. If you quit, write the reallocation plan for the freed hours so you do not quit into a vacuum.

Repeat this worksheet quarterly for your major bets. Conditions change. A Dip can become a cul-de-sac when an industry shifts. A cul-de-sac can reveal a hidden Dip when a new market appears. The point of The Dip is not a one-time inspirational read. It is a habit of strategic choice: quit the wrong curves fast, choose scarce excellence on purpose, and push hard only where pushing can make you best in a world that matters.

Keep the sheet short enough to reuse: market, curve type, scarcity prize, pride risk, decision, and next proof metric. Review it on a calendar. Without review, impulse retakes the wheel.

Lesson: Use a repeatable written test — market, curve type, scarcity, pride bias, and opportunity cost — to decide whether to quit, reposition, or push through.

questions.question_text: In The Dip, what does “best in the world” primarily mean?
questions.option_a: Literally beating every person on the planet at every skill
questions.option_b: Being the best option in a defined market your audience actually considers
questions.option_c: Being popular on social media regardless of craft

questions.question_text: What is the Dip according to Seth Godin?
questions.option_a: A permanent dead end where effort never improves outcomes
questions.option_b: A sudden collapse after everything looked fine
questions.option_c: The hard valley between easy beginner progress and mastery that filters out most people

questions.question_text: What should you do when you recognize a cul-de-sac?
questions.option_b: Quit, because more effort will not create a path to being best
questions.option_c: Work longer hours doing the same thing without changing strategy
questions.option_d: Wait for a cliff, then decide

questions.question_text: How does Godin distinguish quitting from failing?
questions.option_a: Quitting is strategic reallocation; failing is drifting until you are forced out without a plan
questions.option_b: Quitting is always wrong; failing is noble
questions.option_c: They are identical words for giving up
questions.option_d: Failing means changing audiences; quitting means changing products

questions.question_text: Why does the Dip create value for those who get through it?
questions.option_a: Because suffering itself is what customers pay for
questions.option_b: Because the difficulty creates scarcity of excellence, and scarcity makes winners more valuable
questions.option_c: Because everyone finishes at the same rate
questions.option_d: Because pride automatically turns into profit
